title: Majestic Blunder
summary: Offer the bishop to immobilize the king, then choose the king square that wins the pawn race without allowing stalemate.

nodes.question: Is defending a1 enough?
nodes.explanation: White has Kd2, Be5 and c5 against Kb1, a2 and b7. The tempting bishop defense of a1 permits a drawn liquidation.

nodes.question: Which king square wins after the bishop sacrifice?
nodes.explanation: After Ba1 ...Kxa1, the black king blocks its own a-pawn. White must approach with Kc2, so a later ...b3 check can be answered by capture.

branches.title: Sacrifice the bishop, then choose Kc2
commentary: Begin from the complete six-piece source diagram. The position depends on both black pawns and the exact white king square.
Ba1 offers the bishop on the promotion square and puts the black king in zugzwang.
Kxa1 accepts the bishop. Black’s king now blocks its own a2 pawn, giving White time to improve the king.
Kc2 is the essential king placement: it keeps the black king confined and will be able to capture on b3.
b5 is the forced pawn advance, since Ka1 and a2 cannot move.
c6 starts the promotion race while White declines the en passant distraction.
b4 advances again, trying to reach promotion with check.
c7 brings White’s pawn one step from promotion.
b3+ gives check, but the king on c2 can now capture the pawn.
Kxb3 removes Black’s active passer. This is the point that the alternative Kc1 route cannot reproduce in time.
Kb1 clears a1 for Black’s last pawn, but also places the king on the second-rank mating net.
c8=Q promotes first and prepares a check along the c-file.
a1=Q gives Black a queen too. The exact king placement still allows a forced immediate finish.
Qc2# is actual mate. Kb3 protects c2 and covers a2/b2, Qc2 covers a1 and c1, and Black’s own queen occupies a1.
branches.explanation: Qc2# is actual mate. Kb3 protects c2 and covers a2/b2, Qc2 covers a1 and c1, and Black’s own queen occupies a1.

branches.title: Choose Kc1 and take en passant
commentary: Compare the source’s tempting Kc1 blockade after the bishop has been captured.
Kc1 gives up the forced win. It traps the black king, but cannot handle the coming pawn race as Kc2 does.
b5 is a legal two-square move and offers an en passant capture immediately.
cxb6 en passant is actual stalemate: Ka1 is blocked by its own a2 pawn, and Kc1 controls b1 and b2. Black is not in check.
branches.explanation: cxb6 en passant is actual stalemate: Ka1 is blocked by its own a2 pawn, and Kc1 controls b1 and b2. Black is not in check.

branches.title: Defend a1 with Bg7
commentary: Compare the source’s natural bishop defense instead of the zugzwang sacrifice.
Bg7 protects a1 along the diagonal, but this move gives away the exact win.
a1=Q sacrifices the pawn for the bishop guarding promotion.
Bxa1 captures the new queen, but Black can take the bishop next.
Kxa1 captures the bishop, completing the exchange of Black’s a-pawn for White’s bishop. The remaining king-and-pawn position is exactly drawn; the source’s longer pawn chase is not assumed forced.
branches.explanation: Kxa1 captures the bishop, completing the exchange of Black’s a-pawn for White’s bishop. The remaining king-and-pawn position is exactly drawn; the source’s longer pawn chase is not assumed forced.

exercises.prompt: Why is Kc2 more useful than Kc1?
exercises.answer: After ...b5 c6 ...b4 c7 ...b3+, Kc2 can capture b3. From c1 the check costs White a move, so Black’s passer survives.

exercises.prompt: Why decline an available en passant capture?
exercises.answer: After Kc1 ...b5 cxb6 en passant, Black has no legal move and is not in check. Removing the active pawn creates an immediate stalemate.

startContext: The complete six-piece starting position is visually reconstructed. The main source line uses Ba1 ...Kxa1 Kc2 and reaches actual queen mate. Selected comparisons show en passant stalemate after Kc1, and the drawn Bg7 promotion liquidation. All encoded positions are checked exactly.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
